paras: The Slocum massacre was the killing of Black residents by armed white men around Slocum and Denson Springs, south of Palestine in Anderson County, Texas, beginning on the night of July 29, 1910. Sheriff Black estimated fifteen to twenty dead, "all of them probably unarmed," while the grand jury later found eight Black men killed and no white person hurt. Seven white men were indicted for murder, and Black papers called it the "Palestine Massacre."

Accounts of the cause differed. Sheriff Black traced it to a promissory note that R. Afford, a white man, had signed for a Black man who refused to pay it and cursed him. Wire reports added rumors that Black residents had met secretly to plan burning white farmers' houses and killing James Spurger. A Black correspondent in Palestine wrote that no cause had been established beyond a Black man having "sassed" a white man.

The sheriff first heard of trouble late on Friday, July 29, when the Houston County sheriff reported two Black men killed near the county line. According to a New York Sun account, mobs then rode "from cabin to cabin" through the night, shooting Black men, and kept on through Saturday on the roads and in the fields.

Returning after twenty-four hours in the district, Sheriff Black said men "were going about killing negroes as fast as they could find them." He found eleven bodies, four in one house where three men had been sitting up with a dead man, and two in a road with bundles of clothes, as if fleeing. His deputies found only nine single-barreled shotguns in Black homes, none recently fired. He put the mob at 200 to 300 men, mostly from Houston County, while Deputy Sheriff Reeves said no more than fifteen took part. Governor Campbell sent rangers and militia, and District Judge B. H. Gardner closed the saloons and stopped gun sales.

Four white men were jailed on murder charges on July 31, eight by August 1, and a coroner's inquest over eight bodies returned verdicts of death at the hands of "persons unknown." On August 17 the grand jury reported seven Black men killed in Anderson County and one in Houston County, and no white men killed or injured. It indicted seven white men, among them Jim and Curtis Spurger, B. J. and Steve Jenkins, Isom Garner and Andrew Kirkwood, on twenty-two first-degree murder charges covering five victims. No indictments were returned for the killings of John Hayes and Alex Holly.
The defendants faced an examining trial at Crockett for the killing of Will Burley in Houston County. No report of a trial or verdict was found.

The first dispatches described a "race riot" with twenty Black men killed and three white men wounded. The Iowa Bystander, a Black weekly, then reported "Eighteen Blacks and Three Whites" killed in a "pitched battle," and the Washington Bee printed a story of soldiers killed. The Palestine Daily Herald called such reports "absolutely manufactured," and a Black correspondent in Palestine wrote to the Bee that its account was "wildly exaggerated."

In much of the white press, the sheriff's statement set the tone, under headlines such as "Hunts Down and Kills 20 Unarmed Negroes." The Salt Lake Herald-Republican wrote that "the negroes were unarmed and the killing was easy," and a Bee roundup quoted Associated Press accounts calling it "just murder." The Palestine Daily Herald, by contrast, relayed officers' description of a "pot-shot occasion" and worried about the county's "very undesirable advertising."

The New York Age compared the killings to the Kishinev massacre and predicted the "murderers" would be "turned loose." The Richmond Planet printed the sheriff's statement in full and called it "a brutal slaughter of helpless unarmed people." The Cleveland Gazette quoted the Plain Dealer calling "race war" a "handy and high sounding designation" for massacre.

Other counts ran from ten (officers) to twenty (the New York Sun). The inquest, the grand jury and the Black correspondent gave eight; the grand jury's figure, after hearing "witnesses by the hundreds," is the latest and only sworn count. Reports of white casualties appear only in early dispatches and were denied by local officers and the grand jury.

reader.title: Slocum massacre
bases: Armed white men went through the Black settlements around Slocum and Denson Springs over a night and a day, killing Black residents at their homes and on the roads, not a single accused person (A1, A9, A12, A26).

The sheriff's statement, the local Palestine Daily Herald, a coroner's inquest, the grand jury report and a Black correspondent in Palestine all agree that white men killed several Black people and no whites were hurt (A6, A7, A9, A26, A30); early reports of a pitched battle with white dead were later denied (A11, A26).

framing.detail: The sheriff's statement ran widely under headlines such as 'Hunts Down and Kills 20 Unarmed Negroes' and 'Texas Mob Hunts Down and Kills 25 Negroes'.
Early Houston dispatches called it a 'race riot' with white men wounded, tracing it to a quarrel over a note.
The Salt Lake Herald-Republican's 'Murder in Texas' said the victims were unarmed and the killing was 'easy'.
The Palestine Daily Herald accepted that Black men had been killed but concentrated on denying a 'pitched battle' and on the county's 'undesirable advertising'.
The New York Age's 'The Palestine Massacre' compared it to Kishinev and predicted the killers would go free; the Liberator ran the same text.
The Richmond Planet called it 'a brutal slaughter of helpless unarmed people' and urged Black men to own homes and guns.
The Cleveland Gazette and the Washington Bee quoted white papers rejecting the 'race war' label as cover for massacre.
The Iowa Bystander and the Washington Bee printed the early 'pitched battle' version with white casualties.
